scenes.title:
Old spacecraft.
A new way in.
scenes.body:
A mobile companion for amateur radio
and satellite hobbyists.
subs: Satellite hobbyists need to know when to look, where to point, and how the radio frequency shifts.
zombieSatellite brings those steps together on a phone, giving forgotten spacecraft a new role in hands-on learning.

scenes.title:
Seven satellites.
Documented history.
scenes.body:
Explore the people and discoveries
behind the zombie satellites.
scenes.note: Historical receptions are not app activity.
subs: The archive covers seven zombie satellites, with documented stories and sources. Five support playable sessions.
For example, radio amateur Scott Tilley rediscovered the IMAGE spacecraft in twenty eighteen.

scenes.title:
Put the orbit
in your view.
scenes.body:
Use the phone camera as a backdrop
for the computed satellite direction.
scenes.note: This recording shows the app on a phone.
subs: The augmented reality view places the calculated satellite direction over the phone camera.
Switch spacecraft to explore their different positions. The camera is a visual backdrop, not a radio receiver.

scenes.title:
See where
to look.
scenes.body:
Sky view, direction cues and orbit arcs
help you orient the phone.
scenes.note: Below-horizon objects are labelled in the app.
subs: Without the camera, the sky view still shows orbit geometry and direction cues.
These cues help you orient the phone, including when the selected satellite is outside the view.

scenes.title:
Know when
to begin.
scenes.body:
Choose a spacecraft and inspect
its next pass over your location.
scenes.note: Pass times are shown in UTC.
subs: Public orbital data and the observer location determine the next predicted pass. Times are shown in coordinated universal time.
Choose a satellite, inspect the pass, and open its session. Observer coordinates are hidden here for privacy.

scenes.title:
A whole pass.
At 60x speed.
scenes.body:
Practise the session with auto-point
before trying it in real time.
scenes.note: Accelerated simulation of a predicted pass.
subs: This demonstration plays a predicted pass at sixty times normal speed, with automatic pointing enabled.

scenes.title:
Watch the
Doppler shift.
scenes.body:
The displayed kHz value follows
the computed orbital motion.
subs: During the pass, the lock indicator shows pointing accuracy, while the Doppler readout tracks the computed frequency shift.
The beacon sound is synthesized. The app receives no satellite radio signal. Real reception requires your own radio.

scenes.title:
Finish the pass.
Review the result.
scenes.body:
See locked time, lock ratio
and best pointing error.
scenes.note: Results here come from demo mode.
subs: At the end of the pass, review locked time, lock ratio, and pointing error, then open the card collection.

scenes.title:
Keep a record
of the experience.
scenes.body:
QSL cards record the satellite,
timing and session details.
scenes.note: Cards explicitly distinguish simulation from RF.
subs: Each completed session produces a Q S L card containing the satellite, timing, and session details.
Every card identifies the session as simulated, so it cannot be mistaken for proof of radio reception.

scenes.title:
Spec by spec.
Then into code.
scenes.body:
Feature requirements, design and tasks
are kept alongside the implementation.
subs: The project was built with Kiro, using eleven feature specifications and two steering files.
Requirements, design, and tasks structure the work. Steering documents define project scope and development rules.
This evidence is included in the repository, covering orbit prediction, pointing, sessions, and the app shell.

scenes.title:
The orbit is real.
The beacon
is simulated.
scenes.body:
Try a pass on your phone.
Bring your own radio for real listening.
subs: zombieSatellite makes the first steps of satellite tracking accessible on a phone. The orbit is real. The beacon is simulated.
